Building irishQwen · Day 1: Setup04

Setting Up to Program Qwen3

  1. Git account
    • Will help walk through setup (how you will show off your own version afterwards)
  2. Git (legendarily tricky to use)
    • Can use in the command line
    • Can use the GitHub GUI app (easier)
    • Can be used directly through Cursor/VS Code if installed
    • Can be used directly in the browser through github.dev
  3. Code Editor
    • Cursor (what I'll be using) (AI-powered editor just acquired by SpaceX for 60B): used to be free for students, potentially worth paying for if you write a lot of code, though not as attractive as it was 1–2 years ago
    • VS Code (industry standard)
    • github.dev (easiest setup by far)
    • Notepad++ (pretty awful)
    • vim/emacs (if you're a sicko and want to show off) (what I used to use in grad school)
  4. Python
    • Should be installed already if you have a Mac
    • We may just do this in the browser via GitHub Codespaces depending on their compute
  5. Terminal Emulator
    • Terminal.app on Mac (built in)
    • iTerm2 (what I use)
    • Windows Terminal + WSL on Windows
    • Can probably just use in the browser if using github.dev
Building irishQwen · Day 1: Setup05

Git and GitHub

Git is a type of version control software, you can imagine this as "Google Docs" for code.

GitHub is the most popular website for storing your code on. Code projects are stored in "repositories".

Git is THE industry standard for this, when Zach mentioned a "monorepo" and fixing merge requests, he was talking about using git.

Making changes to code with git goes through four main steps:

  1. Create the repository locally: git clone
  2. Make your code changes
  3. add the changes to git: git add -A
  4. commit the changes to git locally: git commit -m "my code changes"
  5. push the changes to git remotely: git push origin master (often main instead of master)
  6. If there are remote changes, you can pull them: git pull

Producing the output prediction: SwiGLU

Building irishQwen · Day 2: SwiGLU16

Three Activations

ReLU, GELU and SiLU, the gate SwiGLU uses

ReLU max(0, x): hard cutoff. For x < 0 the output and the gradient are both exactly 0, so a unit that stays negative stops learning.

GELU x · Φ(x): GPT-2's choice. Φ is the normal CDF. A soft ReLU with a small dip below zero.

SiLU x · σ(x): also called Swish. Almost the same shape as GELU, and its gradient is not zero for x < 0.

Read SiLU as x times σ(x): the number itself, scaled by a 0 to 1 gate computed from that same number.

Building irishQwen · Day 3: Training20

Predicted Training Time

If I tried to train irishQwen at the scale that Alibaba trained their Qwen3-0.6B on my Mac mini (M4, 10-core GPU, 32 GB RAM) it would take approximately 15,500 years of running continuously, without even taking into account heat and memory limitations.

Qwen3-0.6B was trained on 36 trillion tokens and it likely cost ~$250,000 to do the full training run.
